# Kevaṭṭa Sutta (DN 11 (PTS DN i 211))

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kevaṭṭa Sutta* (also known as the *Kevaddha Sutta*, DN 11) is the eleventh discourse of the *Dīghanikāya* [Fiordalis, Miracles]. Set in Nālandā, the discourse begins when the householder Kevaṭṭa urges the Buddha to have a monk perform a miraculous display of psychic powers to inspire devotion in the populace [Fiordalis 2008]. The Buddha firmly refuses, stating that displays of psychic power (*iddhi-pāṭihāriya*) and mind-reading (*ādesanā-pāṭihāriya*) can be dismissed by skeptics as mere charms or magic, and commends instead the miracle of instruction or guidance (*anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya*) [Fiordalis, Miracles; Fiordalis 2008; Pande 1974]. He then recounts the tale of a monk who, seeking to learn where the four great physical elements cease without remainder, meditatively visits an ascending hierarchy of heavenly realms up to the Great Brahmā [Pande 1974]. Brahmā privately confesses his ignorance and refers the monk back to the Buddha, who concludes with enigmatic, archaic verses declaring that name, form, and the elements find no footing in non-manifestative, boundless consciousness (*viññāṇaṁ anidassanaṁ*) [Levman 2014; Pande 1974; Sharf, Early Buddhist Accounts].

Scholars have closely analyzed both the literary composition and the philosophical import of the sutta. G. C. Pande identifies the work as a composite of two originally independent sections: an early discourse discussing the three miracles, which is joined abruptly to a late mythological framing that introduces an ascending hierarchy of gods, culminating in very ancient concluding verses [Pande 1974]. The threefold classification of miracles discussed in the text is shared widely across early Buddhist traditions, including the Dharmaguptaka and Mahīśāsaka Vinayas, as well as the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* [Fiordalis, Miracles; Fiordalis 2008]. The sutta's concluding lines on *viññāṇaṁ anidassanaṁ* parallel passages in the *Brahma-nimantanika Sutta* (MN 49) [Sharf, Early Buddhist Accounts] and are referenced in stanza I 92 of Nāgārjuna's *Ratnāvalī* [Tillemans 1992].

Curated parallels include DĀ 24 in the Chinese *Dīrghāgama*, Sanskrit fragment SHT sutta81, and Tibetan versions preserved in the *Upāyikā* (Up 2.027 and Up 7.025), where the seeking monk is identified as Aśvajit (*rTa thul*) [Levman 2014]. Automated matches from DharmaNexus demonstrate extensive Pali-internal text reuse with the *Iddhipāda Saṁyutta* (SN 51), *Tikanipāta* (AN 3, notably AN 3.60), and *Pāthika Sutta* (DN 24) [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language alignments computed by DharmaNexus confirm close matches with the Chinese *Dīrghāgama* (ZH_T01_0001, fascicle 16) and the Tibetan *Upāyikā* (D4094), corroborating the curated parallels, while also identifying shared phrasing in Candrakīrti's *Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya* and the *Mahāvyutpatti* [DharmaNexus].
